lesson.title: Mendel's Law of Segregation: One Allele per Gamete
lesson.summary: Mendel's law of segregation states that the two alleles an individual carries for a gene separate from each other during gamete formation, so that each gamete receives exactly one of the two alleles.
lesson.body:
A gene can exist in alternative forms called alleles. In pea plants, for example, the gene controlling flower color has a purple allele and a white allele. A diploid individual carries two alleles for each gene, one inherited from each parent. Mendel's law of segregation states that these two alleles separate from each other during the formation of gametes, so that each gamete receives only one of the two alleles, never both.

This rule is not just something Mendel guessed at from counting offspring, it has a direct physical basis in exactly what the chromosomal theory of inheritance, covered in the previous chapter, describes. Each gene sits at a specific location, called a locus, on a specific chromosome. The two alleles an individual carries for that gene sit at the same locus on the two homologous chromosomes, one maternal and one paternal. Because homologous chromosomes separate from each other during anaphase I of meiosis, the two alleles at that locus are physically pulled into different daughter cells. Segregation, in other words, is a direct and necessary consequence of how chromosomes behave in meiosis, not an independent rule layered on top of it.

A worked example makes this concrete, using the same purple versus white flower color trait Mendel himself studied in peas. Let P stand for the purple allele, which is dominant, and p stand for the white allele, which is recessive. Consider a plant with genotype Pp. The law of segregation predicts this plant produces two types of gametes in equal proportion, half carrying P and half carrying p. Now cross two such Pp plants together. Each parent contributes one randomly-selected allele, P or p, to each offspring. Lining up the mother's two gamete types, P and p, against the father's two gamete types, P and p, in a small grid gives four equally likely combinations: P from each parent gives PP, P from the mother with p from the father gives Pp, p from the mother with P from the father gives Pp, and p from each parent gives pp. That works out to a genotype ratio of 1 PP to 2 Pp to 1 pp. Since P is dominant over p, both PP and Pp plants show the purple phenotype, while only pp plants show white, giving a phenotype ratio of 3 purple to 1 white. This 3 to 1 ratio is exactly the pattern Mendel observed experimentally, and it is the signature result of segregation acting on a single gene.

This law also explains something that puzzled biologists before Mendel: traits do not blend together across generations the way mixing two paint colors would. Because alleles stay discrete and separate cleanly during gamete formation, a recessive trait like white flowers can disappear entirely in one generation, hidden behind a dominant allele, and then reappear unchanged in a later generation, exactly as Mendel found when white flowers reappeared among the offspring of purple-flowered F1 plants.
